clinicalPearls: Describes age-related decline in vestibular function producing chronic unsteadiness and a tendency to falls in older adults
Symptoms are typically mild imbalance and postural instability rather than discrete vertigo attacks
Diagnostic criteria require mild bilateral vestibular reduction on quantitative testing that falls short of the thresholds for bilateral vestibulopathy
It is a diagnosis reached after excluding other treatable vestibular and neurological causes of imbalance in the elderly
The deficit reflects gradual loss of vestibular hair cells and neurones as part of normal ageing
Vestibular rehabilitation and multifactorial falls-prevention measures are the mainstays of management
It frequently coexists with presbyacusis, visual decline, and peripheral neuropathy, compounding balance impairment
reference.pathophysiology: With ageing there is progressive attrition of vestibular hair cells, primary vestibular neurones, and otolithic structures, together with reduced central compensation capacity. This produces a mild, symmetrical reduction in vestibular reflexes that impairs the vestibulo-ocular and vestibulospinal contributions to gaze and postural stability. Because the loss is gradual and moderate, patients experience chronic unsteadiness rather than acute vertigo, and the disability is amplified when other age-related sensory systems, particularly vision and proprioception, also decline, reducing the redundancy the balance system relies on for compensation.
additionalDifferentials: Bilateral vestibulopathy with more severe reflex loss
Orthostatic hypotension and cardiovascular causes of unsteadiness
additionalInvestigations: Video head impulse testing to quantify mild reduction in vestibulo-ocular reflex gain
Caloric or rotational chair testing to confirm mild bilateral hypofunction
Assessment of gait, balance, and falls risk
Review of vision, proprioception, and medications contributing to instability
Neuroimaging when central or cerebrovascular disease is suspected
redFlags: Focal neurological signs suggesting a central cause
Rapid deterioration inconsistent with gradual ageing
Severe reflex loss meeting criteria for bilateral vestibulopathy instead
reference.prognosis: The vestibular decline itself is not reversible, but rehabilitation, sensory optimisation, and falls-prevention strategies meaningfully reduce instability and injury risk in most older adults.
pitfalls: Labelling all elderly dizziness as ageing and missing a treatable cause such as positional vertigo
Overlooking contributory medications and cardiovascular factors
Not distinguishing mild age-related loss from true bilateral vestibulopathy
Neglecting the compounding effect of coexisting vision and proprioceptive decline
references: Barany Society Consensus: Presbyvestibulopathy Diagnostic Criteria
